summary:
Our project consists of developing an interactive lunar landing site visualizer that integrates real data from official sources to analyze the Artemis program's South Pole candidate regions and the 6 historic Apollo mission sites. In doing so, we address the challenge of evaluating and comparing complex lunar terrain under extreme lighting conditions, permanent shadows, and rugged topography—critical factors for safe navigation and surface operations planning.
The tool is specifically designed for kids and the general public, aiming to bring space exploration closer in an educational and accessible way. Through the simulator, users learn how different variables—such as terrain slope, solar power generation, and access to strategic resources—determine the viability of a crewed mission. As a final challenge on the site, the platform puts everything learned to the test: users must analyze the data and make their own decisions to execute a successful landing, thereby understanding the real challenges of humanity's sustainable return to the Moon.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Lunaris is an interactive 3D Moon simulator. Users explore 15 lunar South Pole landing candidate sites, adjust time to see solar elevation, temperature and Earth visibility, and use a 360° horizon view to check shadows and direct-to-Earth communication. Six missions, one per Apollo landing (11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17), place markers on the Moon that open photos and curious facts. It runs on precalculated NASA data, so it needs no backend.

What benefits does it have?

It loads instantly, runs on modest hardware and turns dense NASA datasets into something visual and playful. It also shows real lunar conditions, such as temperatures from about 40 K to 130 K and the slopes that matter for landing.

What is the intended impact?

To improve space exploration literacy among students, teachers and enthusiasts, and to explain often-misunderstood phenomena like libration and the low sun angles at the South Pole, linking Apollo history to Artemis.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

React, Vite, TypeScript, React Three Fiber, Drei, Three.js, Tailwind CSS and Electron for the desktop app. For data we used Python (Pandas) with NASA LOLA, JPL Horizons and Moon Trek, exported as static JSON and CSV.

How is your project creative?

It pairs a global 3D view with a first-person horizon view, and turns each Apollo landing into a mission explored through photo markers and curious facts instead of static spreadsheets.

What factors did your team consider?

We chose precalculated data over live queries to avoid latency within 48 hours. We kept the scope on lunar landing sites and communication, and grounded all data in official NASA Artemis and Apollo records.
